name: Bone-extending procedures
lead: Bone-extending procedures, usually called limb lengthening, leg lengthening or height surgery, add stature by lengthening the leg bones. A surgeon cuts the tibia (shin) or femur (thigh bone) and the pieces are separated gradually so new bone forms in the gap, a method called distraction osteogenesis [1]. People choose it to gain permanent height and, in some cases, to correct leg shape or body proportion [2]. It is the one height-increasing approach that changes the skeleton itself rather than footwear, posture or presentation.

The technique grew out of work by Gavriil Ilizarov from the 1950s, who developed external fixators and workable separation rates [1][2]. The first reported cosmetic case, in Volgograd in 1992, lengthened a healthy patient's tibia by 6 cm over 11 months [2]. Current options include external ring frames, lengthening over a nail, and fully implantable motorized nails such as the Fitbone and Precice [1][8].

A 2020 systematic review of cosmetic stature lengthening pooled 11 case series covering 795 patients and reported a mean gain of 6.7 cm and high satisfaction, with major complications described as rare [9]. Other series and commentators emphasise that complications are common and that patients need counselling and psychological screening [10][11]. Height surgery has also drawn media attention, including a 2026 New York Times article titled "Height Surgery for Men Can Add Inches but Has Risks" [3].

angle.text: Surgeons lengthen the tibia or femur by gradual distraction, producing a lasting gain in standing height; the first cosmetic case added 6 cm [2]. It is the route people take when they want added height that does not depend on footwear or posture, and it can also change leg-to-torso proportion [2].

paras: Distraction osteogenesis has five phases: osteotomy, in which the bone is cut and the device fitted; a latency period of about seven days; distraction at roughly 1 mm per day, usually in two steps; consolidation while the new bone hardens; and removal of the device in a second operation [1].

Devices include manually turned external rods, spring-tensioned frames that separate bones continuously, and the Fitbone, a fully implantable motorized nail. Wikipedia's summary lists accurate correction, less scar tissue and lower infection risk among the Fitbone's reported advantages, and says patients report it as more comfortable than mechanical systems [1].

Timing matters biologically. Wikipedia's distraction osteogenesis article says that if separation is too fast the gap can fill with unstable fibrous tissue instead of bone, and if too slow the bone can unite prematurely, which is why the rate of about 1 mm per day and its rhythm are fixed at the start of treatment.[5] Manual devices turn a rod that drives a rack-and-pinion mechanism, and some use springs for continuous tension.[5]

Anthropometric cosmetology lists indications including legs short relative to body length, X- or O-shaped leg curvature, and distress about height [2]. Operations are professionally recommended from age 17, after the growth zones have closed [2].

Guerreschi and Tsibidakis describe candidates below the 5th percentile for age and sex without dwarfism, skeletal deformity or hormone deficiency, and consider 5 to 8 cm of bilateral lengthening satisfactory; patients in their series reported better self-esteem, less shyness and better quality of life [11]. Functional limits of short stature, such as difficulty with large bicycles or motorcycles, were treated as a valid reason in that series [11].
In India, where height is described as highly attractive and linked to marriage and career prospects, cosmetic lengthening has been in demand [1].

Lengthening was developed for unequal leg length, deformity and fracture non-union, and is used for conditions such as achondroplasia. Since the 1980s the most common use of distraction osteogenesis has been in jaw and skull conditions [5][8]. Hosny's 2020 history notes that indications have expanded to arm and hand lengthening and to cosmetic lengthening, the latter requiring careful psychological evaluation [8].

Hosny's review traces devices from skeletal traction and unilateral fixators through circular Ilizarov and hexapod frames (including the Taylor Spatial Frame), to lengthening over small nails, to internal nails. The Albizzia nail used a ratchet needing limb rotation; the ISKD was cleared in the US in 2001 and later withdrawn after complications from uncontrolled distraction; Fitbone and Precice are motorized nails that do not need rotation and are increasingly used [8].

In the 2020 systematic review of cosmetic lengthening, classic three- or four-ring Ilizarov fixators were used in 33.6% of patients, lengthening over nail in 31.8% and implantable lengthening nails in 7.9%. The nail group had the shortest treatment time and fewest problems per patient, though the authors found none of the between-technique differences statistically significant [9]. A nine-patient series of cosmetic bilateral nail lengthening reported a mean gain of 8.7 cm and a 22% complication rate, and eight of nine patients said they would repeat it [12].

sections.h: The Ilizarov method and external frames
paras: The Ilizarov apparatus is a modular external frame of stainless steel or titanium rings held to healthy bone with wires and pins and joined by threaded rods. Adjusting the rods about four times a day separates the healing bone by roughly 1 mm per day, after which the frame stays on while the new bone hardens, and a second operation removes it.[6] Wikipedia says Ilizarov originally developed it for non-union fractures, discovered distraction osteogenesis when a frame was accidentally lengthened rather than shortened, and that it reached US medicine in 1987; the Taylor Spatial Frame is a later development.[6]

Leg lengthening with these frames can require an additional operation to lengthen the Achilles tendon, and reported complications include inflammation, muscle damage from the pins and joint contracture.[6] Wikipedia names Soviet high-jump champion Valeriy Brumel, whose leg was lengthened 3.5 cm after his ankle failed to heal, and explorer Carlo Mauri among Ilizarov's best-known patients.[6]

Bernhard von Langenbeck proposed bone lengthening in 1869, and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, treating 26 people with high complication rates [1]. Abbott reported lower-limb lengthening in 73 patients in 1932 and set out principles such as a waiting period before distraction [8]. Ilizarov began working with a circular frame and tensioned wires in 1951, studied the method in more than 15,000 people, and defined optimal distraction rates [1][8]. In 1965 he determined that bone fragments could be pulled apart without losing alignment [2].

Kaplunov and Yegorov used the method for strictly cosmetic purposes in Volgograd in 1992, lengthening a healthy patient's tibia by 6 cm over 11 months; Yegorov, Chernov and Nekrasov later wrote the first scientific book on the field, Orthopedic Cosmetology [2]. The Russian Ilizarov Scientific Centre later reported a retrospective series of 138 cosmetic patients treated between 1983 and 2006 [10].

Marwan and colleagues (Bone & Joint Research, 2020) reviewed 11 studies of 795 patients, all case series or retrospective reviews. Mean gain was 6.7 cm (range 1.5 to 13 cm) with mean follow-up of 4.9 years; ankle equinus was the most common problem, and regenerate deformation and subtalar stiffness were the most common complications. Most patients were satisfied, one study reported 94% satisfaction, and one found self-esteem gains at one year had returned to preoperative levels by seven years. The authors called for clear indications, contraindications and guidelines [9].

Novikov and colleagues reported 131 patients (mean age 25, mean preoperative height 159 cm) with bilateral Ilizarov lengthening between 1983 and 2006. Mean gain was 6.9 cm (males 7.3, females 6.5), mean frame time 215 days, and outcomes were rated excellent in 55% and good in 40%; 37% of patients had complications and 18% needed reoperation. The authors advised extreme caution and preoperative counselling [10].

Guerreschi and Tsibidakis reported 63 patients (126 legs) treated with Ilizarov hybrid frames between 1985 and 2010, with a mean gain of 7.2 cm over about 9.5 months. Of 126 legs, 102 had difficulties (42 problems, 54 obstacles and 6 complications), pin-tract infection was the most common problem, and pin-site scars were a main source of dissatisfaction; outcomes were excellent in 88.8% [11].

A 2023 evaluation of 51 websites about limb lengthening found average quality scores that the authors described as low (DISCERN 33.9 of 80), with academic sites scoring higher than commercial ones [13]. A secret-shopper study that posed as a 35-year-old man seeking elective stature lengthening contacted 27 practices; only 3 answered every scripted question, and cost estimates ranged widely, in the tens of thousands of dollars [14]. The authors recommended standardised, transparent online information [14].

For distraction osteogenesis in general, Wikipedia cites overall infection of 5%, bone growing in the wrong direction in 7-9%, hardware failure in 3-4.5% and protocol failure in 4.5% [1]. Early operations by Codivilla in 1905 had high rates of infection, tissue death and failed union [5].

Cosmetic series report ankle equinus and knee flexion deformity, pin-tract infection, nerve palsy, delayed or deformed regenerate, osteomyelitis and in rare cases fracture through new bone [9][10][11]. Authors of cosmetic series list nerve damage, loss of joint mobility, infection, impaired bone healing and death as risks that patients should be told about [14]. Pin-site scarring with external frames is reported as a cosmetic downside [11]. Authors of the nail series note complications such as insufficient regeneration, quadriceps contracture and screw pull-out [12].

In India, some patients reported that surgeons misled them about complications, and some who developed infections needed further surgery months later to walk again; some gained less height than expected [1]. China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after operations with serious side effects [1]. Authors of cosmetic series also describe ethical objections and the need for psychological screening, including for body dysmorphic disorder [11].

Height surgery is discussed in height-focused communities as the durable alternative to lifts or posture work, with attention to cost, recovery time and surgeon choice. It also appears in popular media, including a video discussed on Lemmy as a dangerous plastic surgery trend [4] and the Hacker News thread on the 2026 New York Times article [3]. Because insurance usually does not cover cosmetic surgery, authors note cost is a barrier [11].

In India, cosmetic limb lengthening is described as in high demand and unregulated, with patients as young as 13 or 14 reported, and some patients saying surgeons understated the risks; one surgeon criticised the short training of practitioners.[5] China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006.[5] The 1997 film Gattaca uses leg lengthening in its plot.[5]

Cosmetic lengthening has been examined in retrospective case series rather than randomised trials: a 2020 systematic review of 11 studies (795 patients) [9], a 131-patient Ilizarov series [10], a 63-patient hybrid-frame series [11] and a 9-patient nail series [12]. Complication figures for distraction osteogenesis more broadly come from lengthening for deformity and trauma [1][8].

lore.intro: In height-focused communities and media, limb lengthening is discussed as the durable option for added height, alongside concerns about cost, recovery and risk [3][4].

claims.claim: Leg lengthening gives permanent height of several centimetres
claims.believers: Patients and surgeons describe lasting gains, with the first cosmetic case adding 6 cm [2].
claims.experts: A systematic review reported a mean gain of 6.7 cm (range 1.5 to 13 cm) at mean follow-up of 4.9 years; one series reported mean 6.9 cm [9][10].

claims.believers: Patients in published series report better self-esteem, less shyness and better quality of life [11][12].
claims.experts: Most reviewed studies reported satisfaction, but several used unvalidated measures, and one found self-esteem gains at one year had returned to preoperative levels by seven years [9].

claims.claim: Modern implantable nails make the procedure easier and safer than external frames
claims.believers: Wikipedia's summary lists accurate correction, less scar tissue and lower infection risk among the Fitbone's advantages [1].
claims.experts: In the 2020 review the nail group had the fewest problems and shortest treatment, but differences were not statistically significant; nails have device-specific complications [8][9][12].

claims.believers: Authors of case series describe low rates of major complications [9][11].
claims.experts: One 131-patient series reported complications in 37% and reoperation in 18%, and the authors advised extreme caution [10].

claims.claim: Clinics give patients full information about risks and cost
claims.believers: Clinics advertise outcomes and recovery times online.
claims.experts: A secret-shopper study found only 3 of 27 practices answered every scripted question, and a website evaluation rated most online information as low quality [13][14].

claims.claim: Lengthening surgery is risky enough that some countries restrict it
claims.believers: Critics point to infections and patients who needed further surgery in India [1].
claims.experts: China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after operations with serious side effects [1].

card.summary: Surgery that gradually lengthens leg bones to add permanent height.
card.aka: Limb lengthening, height surgery, leg lengthening
card.note: Major surgery with months of recovery and a recognised complication rate.

quick.overview:
Bone-extending procedures cut a leg bone and slowly pull the ends apart so new bone grows in between. The result is permanent added height, historically several centimetres per bone.

The first cosmetic case in 1992 added 6 cm to a tibia over 11 months.
quick.mechanism: Distraction osteogenesis: osteotomy, a short wait, lengthening of about 1 mm per day with an external frame or motorized nail, then months of bone consolidation.
quick.risks: Reported complications include infection (about 5%), poor bone healing, hardware failure and nerve injury. Regulation varies; China banned the procedure in 2006.
